newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt happy for Chahine, worried about Islamists.
newsitem.headline: Egypt happy for Chahine, worried about Islamists.

text.p: Egyptians on Monday welcomed a Cannes film festival award to veteran director Youssef Chahine but said it would not improve freedom of expression in Egypt.
The Cannes jury on Sunday gave Chahine a special 50th anniversay prize for his life's work, which the director labelled "a hope for future generations" of film-makers.
But a human rights activist said the prize could raise the ire of Islamists who successfully banned a film by Chahine in 1995.
Intellectuals and artists in Egypt complain Islamists are trying to monopolise the moral sphere in Egypt in order to turn the country into a strict Islamic state.

"The prize might encourage state censors to be more liberal but it will not have any positive effect on Islamist censorship. It could form a kind of challenge. I would not be surprised if Islamists tried to ban Chahine's new film 'Destiny'," human rights activist Hisham Mubarak told Reuters.
Chahine was in competition at Cannes with "Destiny", a French-Egyptian co-production that chronicles the trials of 12th century philosopher Averroes who lived in Moslem Spain.
The director told reporters in Cannes that "Destiny" was an appeal for tolerance. Averroes' books were ordered to be burned after a protest by religious fundamentalists.

"Chahine does not have a problem with state censors, he has a good relationship with them. The prize will only have a meaning for intellectuals, liberals and those concerned with civil society," said Mubarak, of the independent Centre for Human Rights Legal Aid.
A court in 1995 banned Chahine's film "The Migrant" after Islamists complained it violated Islamic rules by portraying the story of the patriarch Joseph, whom Moslems consider a prophet.
Chahine, 72, who has been making films for more than four decades, denied the charge, saying the court trial was an attempt to take Egypt back to the dark ages.

Although Chahine had the approval of state censors for the film, which thousands of Egyptians had seen before the ban, the court based its decision on a report by al-Azhar mosque, the Sunni Moslem world's most presigious seat of learning, that said the film told the story of Joseph.

A state censorship board must approve any screenplay before filming begins in Egypt. Politics and sex are the usual taboo subjects but many in the film industry say lack of financing is a greater nemesis than censorship.
